articles.title: Bengaluru’s early tryst with scientific research
articles.summary: C V Raman’s association with Bengaluru , as director of the Indian Institute of Science (IISc) and founder of the Raman Research Institute, is well known. Less familiar, however, is his connection with Central College. Nearly a century ago, on March 16, 1928, the college witnessed a historic moment. Addressing an audience on its campus, Raman announced: “I propose this evening to speak to you on a new kind of radiation or light emission from atoms and molecules.” It was the first public presentation of a discovery that would become famous as the Raman Effect. Two years later, he was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for this discovery, becoming the first Asian to receive a Nobel Prize in science. Central College was a fitting venue for Raman’s announcement of his groundbreaking discovery. By then, the institution had established itself as an important centre of scientific learning and research, particularly in physics. Founded in 1858 by Wesleyan missionary and Kannada scholar Rev John Garrett, Central College began as a high school. In 1875, under principal Charles Waters, it grew into a first-grade college affiliated with the University of Madras, with mathematics and physics in its curriculum. John M A Cook brought a fresh momentum to scientific learning at the college when he took over as principal and head of physics in 1882. Cook also re-established the Mysore Meteorological Observatory on the campus. A telescope made in Berlin in 1884, parts of which still rest on the college verandah, offers a link to that period of scientific activity. A decisive phase in the development of physics at Central College began in 1908, when E P Metcalfe joined as professor and head of the Physics Department. Metcalfe equipped part of the old college building for practical physics. By 1912, the department had a building of its own. Physics, at the time, was overshadowed by applied subjects such as chemistry and geology. Even IISc, established in 1909, set up its physics department only in 1933, with Raman’s arrival. Another milestone came in 1916, when Central College became a constituent of the newly established University of Mysore. Central College emerged as the university’s science campus, with postgraduate science programmes beginning in 1919. Flourishing research culture Spectroscopy was among the areas of physics that prospered during this period, driven by Metcalfe and B Venkatesachar, who joined the college as assistant professor in 1916. They conducted extensive studies on the spectral lines of mercury vapour. Venkatesachar later collaborated with L Sibaiya on research into hyperfine structure — the splitting of spectral lines caused by interactions between atomic nuclei and electrons. Their work helped investigate nuclear spins and identify isotopes of several elements, notably iridium. Activists to form human chain against elevated corridor in Bengaluru's CV Raman Nagar By 1935, Metcalfe also established what is described as India’s first shortwave public entertainment broadcasting station at Central College, which operated under the call sign VU6AH. Wireless research became another active area of study. The Mathematics Department, too, attracted notable scholars. B S Madhava Rao, a well-known mathematician and theoretical physicist who later became the college principal, joined the department in the 1920s. He went on to work with Max Born on field theory and with Homi J Bhabha on the wave equations of mesons, subatomic particles whose existence had only recently been predicted. Scientific activity at Central College was not confined to laboratories and academic publications. Bellave Venkatanaranappa, a physicist at the college, played an important role in popularising science. Along with Nangapuram Venkatesha Iyengar, he helped establish the Karnataka Vijnana Pracharini Samiti in 1917. The following year, the Samiti launched its magazine, Vijnana, to take popular science to Kannada readers. A new radiation It was in this intellectually vibrant setting that Raman presented and explained the significance of his discovery, which had been just announced to the press on February 28. The occasion was the inaugural address at the eighth annual session of the South Indian Science Association, organised jointly with the Central College Science Club. Drawing on research conducted at the Indian Association for the Cultivation of Science in Calcutta, with K S Krishnan and others, Raman presented experimental observations of the Raman Effect. The lecture was published in the Indian Journal of Physics on March 31, the same day that Nature carried the paper by Raman and Krishnan titled “A New Type of Secondary Radiation”. Central College’s contribution to physics research continued in the decades that followed. In the late 1940s, Homi J Bhabha, then at IISc, conducted early cosmic-ray experiments at Central College. Enduring legacy The college also produced several prominent scientists and intellectuals, including three Bharat Ratna awardees — Sir M Visvesvaraya, C Rajagopalachari and C N R Rao. Among its distinguished alumni were physicists such as Rajeshwari Chatterjee, the first woman faculty member at IISc, who pioneered microwave engineering research in India, and Hosur Narasimhaiah, who became a noted educator and advocate of rationalism. When Central College became affiliated to Bangalore University in the 1960s, its Physics Department moved to the Jnanabharathi campus. The department restarted in the old physics building after the college became part of Bengaluru City University in 2017. Today, the college continues to offer postgraduate science education, with research continuing in many departments despite the several constraints it faces. Raman Hall, where Raman delivered his historic lecture, still stands on the campus — a reminder of the institution’s contribution to the development of science in Karnataka. articles.title: Pranab Mukherjee nudged Suvendu Adhikari to quit Mamata's party and join Modi
articles.summary: Kolkata: Pranab Mukherjee , despite rising to the highest constitutional office in the country, reached the end of his long political career with a sense of discontent, and he apparently did not want Suvendu Adhikari to endure the same agony. So, he advised Suvendu to leave the Trinamool Congress and join the Bharatiya Janata Party if he wanted to rise and shape his own political career instead of remaining on the second rung of Mamata Banerjee’s party. That, at least, is what Suvendu, now the Chief Minister of West Bengal , has claimed of late. “Stay where you are if you want to remain an ‘employee’ or go with Modi Ji (Prime Minister Narendra Modi) if you want to move ahead on your own,” Suvendu quoted Mukherjee as telling him during one of their meetings in New Delhi. The Chief Minister of the BJP government in West Bengal did not reveal when the 13th President of the country offered him this advice. “I don’t want to speak much on this as a controversy may be created,” he said at an event in Kolkata, adding: “He (Mukherjee) is no more amongst us. He was a guardian, an advisor. People across the country respected him, cutting across political lines.” Suvendu had indeed acted on Mukherjee's ‘advice’. He eventually quit the TMC and joined the BJP in December 2020, a few months after Mukherjee had died of Covid-19. His account of Mukherjee’s advice to him to switch allegiance to Modi came about a fortnight after Sonia Gandhi’s memoir, Belonging: A Journey of Love, revived interest in the late Congress veteran’s own prime ministerial ambitions and the sense of discontent he was long believed to have harboured over not receiving the political rewards he might have felt his decades of loyalty to the grand old party deserved. In her memoir, Sonia wrote about a discussion she had with Mukherjee, then External Affairs Minister, in 2010. The veteran leader had been at odds with P Chidambaram, then Finance Minister in Prime Minister Manmohan Singh’s government. He suggested to Sonia, then chairperson of the ruling United Progressive Alliance, that the government might need a change of leadership, a remark she perceived as an indirect expression of his own desire to become Prime Minister. She chose not to pursue the subject, later acknowledging that Mukherjee might have been disappointed, though he never gave her reason to believe that he resented her for it. The Congress had nominated Mukherjee as its candidate for the presidential election in 2012, which he won comfortably. He served as President from July 2012 to July 2017, overseeing the transition from the Singh-led UPA government to the Modi-led National Democratic Alliance government in May 2014. Notwithstanding their contrasting political affiliations, Mukherjee and Modi, as President and Prime Minister, developed a cordial working relationship. Aunt-nephew went to Delhi to seek support from anarchists: Suvendu targets Mamata and Abhishek Mukherjee later acknowledged in his farewell address to Parliament that he had greatly benefited from Modi’s advice and cooperation in discharging his constitutional responsibilities. The Modi government subsequently conferred the Bharat Ratna on Mukherjee in 2019, a year after he delivered a lecture at the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh’s headquarters in Nagpur. Mukherjee's association with Suvendu’s family went back several years. He had known Suvendu’s father, Sisir Adhikari, from his days in the Congress in West Bengal. Their association continued even after Sisir moved to the TMC, along with Suvendu. When Suvendu contested his first Lok Sabha election from Tamluk in 2009, Mukherjee travelled by helicopter from Purulia to Mahishadal to campaign for him. The Congress and the TMC had forged an alliance for the Lok Sabha elections. At a rally, Mukherjee publicly vouched for Suvendu's integrity and urged voters to elect him. Suvendu, who had switched from the Congress to the TMC in 1998, emerged as one of Mamata Banerjee’s most influential lieutenants, playing a key role in the party’s rise through the agitation in Nandigram in 2007-08. Nandigram, in the Purba Medinipur district, had become a watershed in West Bengal politics after farmers protested the Left Front government's proposed acquisition of around 10,000 acres for the Salim Group of Indonesia to set up a chemical industries hub. The agitation turned violent, culminating in the killing of at least 14 people in police firing on March 14, 2007, during a crackdown on protesters. Mamata, along with several social organisations, played a key role in the movement, with Suvendu emerging as one of its prominent political faces. The agitation became a defining battle against the Left Front, which had ruled the state for 34 years, and helped propel the TMC to power in 2011, bringing Mamata to the Chief Minister’s office. Suvendu won the Tamluk Lok Sabha seat in 2009 and 2014 before returning to state politics as the legislator from Nandigram in 2016 and becoming a minister in the state government headed by Mamata. I did not want to remain as an employee, so I quit,” Suvendu said just before claiming that he had acted in accordance with Mukherjee’s advice.

articles.summary: Even as Dhaka wants New Delhi to send her back in handcuffs, India on Wednesday drew a line between Bangladesh’s request for the extradition of Sheikh Hasina and her plan to return to her country voluntarily on December 16. With Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s government in Dhaka drifting into Beijing’s sphere of geopolitical influence, New Delhi is also keeping tabs on the recent seizure of a merchant vessel sailing from China to Bangladesh and carrying over 405 tonnes of sodium perchlorate, which can be used in the manufacture of missile propellants. India also expressed concern over recent reports of attacks on religious minorities in Bangladesh. “The case of a citizen willing to return voluntarily to her country on a travel document is a matter separate from the extradition request,” Randhir Jaiswal, spokesperson for the Ministry of External Affairs, told journalists in New Delhi. He was responding to a query about the Awami League’s announcement that Sheikh Hasina planned to return to Bangladesh on December 16 and Dhaka’s renewed demand that New Delhi send her “in handcuffs or under strict surveillance”. New Delhi distanced itself from the Awami League chief’s plan, with the MEA spokesperson underlining that the former Bangladesh prime minister’s proposed return from India was a matter between her and the government of her country. Jaiswal also reiterated that New Delhi was examining Dhaka’s request for the extradition of the deposed prime minister in line with the “established processes”. Hasina’s Awami League on Tuesday announced that Bangladesh’s deposed prime minister would return to her country from India on December 16, a date carefully chosen for its historical and political significance, as well as to galvanise her party’s cadres at a time when the Bangladesh Nationalist Party’s government is already grappling with unrest in several districts. Bangladesh court sentences Sheikh Hasina to 10 years in jail in corruption cases It was on December 16, 1971, that East Pakistan broke free from Pakistan and emerged as the new nation of Bangladesh. The day is celebrated as Victory Day on both sides of the border, commemorating the surrender of the Pakistan Army’s Eastern Command to the joint command of Indian and Bangladeshi forces, which ended the Muktijuddha. Hasina left Bangladesh a few hours before her Awami League government collapsed amid mass protests. The protests were initially triggered by student and youth demonstrations against the reservation system in government jobs and intensified by a police crackdown on protesters. A court in Dhaka had, on November 17, 2025, sentenced Hasina to death for “crimes against humanity” committed during the police crackdown on protesters in July 2024. Bangladesh’s then interim government subsequently sought her extradition from India. Hasina had said a few months ago that she would return to her country by the end of 2026. She recently sought travel documents from the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi to facilitate her return. According to her spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, her lawyer sent communications to the mission on November 9 and 19 seeking the necessary documents. She also asked the Dhaka government to arrange her return on the national carrier, Biman Bangladesh, arguing that since she was flown to India aboard a Bangladeshi military aircraft on August 5, 2024, the BNP government in Dhaka should facilitate her return on an aircraft operated by the country's national carrier.

articles.title: D Gukesh, Sindarov split points after 20-move draw in Geneva
articles.summary: It was a relatively quiet skirmish as World Champion Dommaraju Gukesh and challenger Javokhir Sindarov of Uzbekistan settled for a draw after just 20 moves in the second game of the Salesforce FIDE World Chess Championship in Geneva , Switzerland . The score now stands at 1-1 after two consecutive draws in this 14-game match. Incidentally, the players had exchanged just one pair of knights, with the remaining pawns and pieces still on the board, as they agreed to a draw by threefold repetition, much to the disappointment of the watching enthusiasts. Sindarov initiated the draw in both games, but Gukesh looked far from pleased with the result on Thursday. The Indian has been consuming plenty of time in the opening stages, and another 30-minute think on the 16th move left Sindarov with 40 minutes more on the clock, a fact that may have weighed heavily on Gukesh's mind as he agreed to the repetition of moves. Gukesh's opening repertoire with White is quite broad-based and keeps his opponent guessing as to whether he will open with the King's Pawn or the Queen's Pawn. Sindarov was briefly surprised by Gukesh's third move, with the Indian opting for the London System in the Queen's Pawn opening. Sindarov later admitted as much but also commented that he had studied the variation played. The slow pace at which both players approached the opening indicated that perhaps they were sailing in uncharted territory and that the game was not very much part of either player's home preparation. Interestingly, the short game was marked by Sindarov retreating and trying to regroup his queen and bishop. Gukesh, too, moved his rook before retreating it to its original square. The queen's retreat to its original square on the 11th move had Gukesh thinking for a long time once again, followed by another half-hour think on the 16th move. FIDE World Championships: D Gukesh dodges early check to hold Uzbekistan's Sindarov It was apparent that, apart from playing the game, Gukesh was also racing against the clock. To give credit to Sindarov, he was quick and precise with the black pieces. Later, at the press conference, when asked about the London Opening, which many find dull and boring, Gukesh commented: “I think it’s a cool opening and I don’t know why it is hated so much online. These days any Opening you play, the opponent is always well prepared and it does not matter which Opening you play”. Gukesh was also quick to point out that he could not think of any promising continuation and was therefore not averse to a draw. Sindarov, on the other hand, had an amusing take when asked why he spent time pacing around while Gukesh was thinking and at times yawned and appeared to take short naps. “I am chilling out but obviously I am thinking and looking at the moves ahead. This is my first experience of a World Championship Match and trying to adjust.” On Thursday, Sindarov will have the white pieces against Gukesh before the players head into a rest day on Friday. He reportedly spoke to his wife and family members over a video call on the night of October 16, after which he could no longer be contacted. When he was also found missing from his workplace, Daisy and Savitha lodged complaints with the Mangaluru City Police Commissioner, local elected representatives and the Indian Embassy in Israel.
